name: Nickel oxyhydroxide
cathode: Nickel oxyhydroxide with manganese dioxide and graphite
summary: Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiOOH, abbreviated NiOx) primary cells add nickel oxyhydroxide to an alkaline cell's manganese dioxide cathode, raising the unloaded voltage to about 1.7 V. They were sold for high-drain devices such as digital cameras under names including Panasonic Oxyride.
body:
## How it works

A nickel oxyhydroxide primary cell is a modified alkaline cell. The anode is zinc and the electrolyte is alkaline, as in an LR cell, but the cathode adds nickel oxyhydroxide to the manganese dioxide and graphite. Wikipedia notes two manufacturing differences: finer-grained graphite in the cathode, and a vacuum pouring process that puts more electrolyte into the cell. EE Power's 2005 report on Panasonic's Oxyride line describes the same cathode recipe and the vacuum electrolyte process.

## Discharge behavior

The unloaded voltage is about 1.7 V, against 1.5 V for alkaline, and the cell holds a higher average voltage during discharge. IEC 60086-1 lists the system at 1.5 V nominal with a maximum open-circuit voltage of 1.78 V. The higher voltage is the main compatibility issue. Wikipedia notes that it can cause problems in equipment with incandescent bulbs, such as flashlights, and in devices without a voltage regulator. It can also give a false reading in equipment that estimates remaining runtime from battery voltage. In low-drain use, life is reported to be similar to alkaline.

## Uses

The chemistry was aimed at high-drain consumer electronics. DV Hardware's report of Panasonic's announcement describes Oxyride as suited to digital still cameras, handheld games and portable audio products, and quotes Panasonic's statement that in independent lab testing AA Oxyride cells lasted twice as long as alkaline cells in digital cameras.

## History

DV Hardware reported Panasonic's Oxyride announcement on July 29, 2005. EE Power reported in December 2005 that Oxyride went on sale to US consumers in July 2005 and, four months later, was available in over 14,000 retail outlets covering about 95% of the United States.

## Status

Legacy. Wikipedia abbreviates the system NiOx. It keeps its own IEC system letter, Z, so a nickel oxyhydroxide AA is designated ZR6, but the sources consulted here do not give a current consumer product line.
strengths: Higher voltage under load than alkaline
Aimed at high-drain devices such as digital cameras
limitations: About 1.7 V unloaded can be too high for incandescent flashlights and unregulated devices
Life similar to alkaline in low-drain use
